about_body_p1: The Human2Human project aims to bring hope and humanity to our fellow humans in the most hurting and isolated places on the planet — in a way that doesn't trouble the health and happiness of animals, fish and other our fellow creatures in the ecosystem. To do so, we've developed the hope turtle: a non-capital, open-source, autonomous marine vehicle that embodies Earthen principles. Turtles are made from locally available and 95% organic materials in such a way that anyone around the world can build them-- and make them better! Rather than relying on centralized, traditional logistics to deliver aid, turtles enable humans to mobilize collective decentralized delivery direct to those who need it most.
about_body_p2: Each Hope Turtle is a buoyant marine vessel built primarily from bamboo and repurposed bottles — materials that are widely available, inexpensive, and biodegradable. Inspired by ancestral Austronesian seafaring traditions, the design harnesses ocean currents, wind, and solar energy rather than fossil fuels. Version 1.0 is a hand-assembled structure that carries six food-filled bottles as payload. Version 2.0 integrates onboard electronics, GPS navigation, telemetry, and self-steering — enabling independent voyages across hundreds of kilometres of open sea.
about_body_p3: Supporting the physical vessels is the hopeTurtles.org human-to-human platform — a transparent, open-source web application that connects senders and recipients directly. People in need can request specific items; supporters around the world respond by packing a bottle, registering it with a unique serial number, and dispatching it. When a turtle arrives, the recipient can look up their sender and share news of its safe arrival — creating a living record of solidarity and connection.
about_body_p4: The project is grounded in Earthen ecological principles and a commitment to radical transparency and non-violence. All designs, source code, and research are publicly available. The vessels are engineered to be as organic and biodegradable as possible — so that even if a turtle ends its journey unexpectedly, it leaves behind nutrition rather than pollution. This regenerative philosophy extends to the platform, the community, and the culture of the project itself.
about_body_p5: The Hope Turtle Project is not simply a technology project — it is an invitation. An invitation to imagine and embody a world in which compassion travels freely across borders and oceans. By keeping costs low and designs open, the project is built to grow: engineers, makers, sailors, and communities everywhere are invited to build their own Hope Turtles, commission deployments, and join a growing global bale of people committed to turning concern into care. Every turtle in the water is a small, humble, powerful act of hope.
about_principle_earth_body: Turtles are made with the health and benefit of the biosphere and the local biome and ecosystem first and foremost. While this focuses on the well being of humans in a particular locale, it also and equally includes the animals, plants and other organisms there too. Mindful of the various species we will benefit (fish, whales, humans) we do not distinguish along human political lines.
about_principle_love_body: Turtles are designed as acts that acknowledge the hurt and needs of locale. Before sending we actively listen and hear the needs of the humans there and contribute in a way that doesn't hurt other humans or actively benefit one group of humans over another.
about_principle_opensource_body: All the code, designs and specs are shared in such a way that they may be copied and used by others along our same principles.
about_principle_locable_body: We use only materials that can be sourced just about anywhere in the world locally (bottles, wood, generic electronics).
about_principle_noncapital_body: Turtles are designed from the ground up, not to rely on capital intensive platforms, technologies or components. Yes, money is still important, but by prioritizing locally sourceable, often discarded materials (PET bottles, pallet wood, etc.) capital does not become a barrier to replicability.
about_principle_spiral_body: We make sure that all of our components and materials can be cycled again in a way that is beneficial over many such cycles for humans, animals and ecosystems. This means using reusable and biodegradable materials just as much as it means avoiding for-profit platforms, technologies and services.
about_consequence_reusable_body: Every element of the turtle can be readily repurposed. From the screws to the wood, from the bottles to the sensor circuits, each element can be removed and reused.
about_consequence_biodegradable_body: The net weight of the turtle will be materials that biodegrade (wood, bamboo, canvas, etc.) or which are inert and non-toxic (steel screws, silicon board). We avoid the use of new plastics as much as possible.
about_consequence_fixable_body: All elements of the turtle are repairable and replaceable, and we maintain documentation on how.
about_consequence_replicable_body: Because our designs are open source, non-capital and locable, they can be readily replicated by folks around the world. As others follow our principles, their work can be replicated also. As we all iterate, our designs get better and better in ways that none of us could foresee.
about_consequence_lowcost_body: Our goal is to keep the net fabrication cost of a turtle below $100.
about_materials_caption: Turtles are designed from the ground up along Earthen principles. By net weight a turtle's materials are 95% organic and its components 100% reusable. This way we don't hurt our fellow creatures while helping our fellow humans.
about_earthen_body: Hope Turtles are based on the regenerative ecological ethos of Earthen ethics.

turtleos_body_p1: Inspired by other great autonomous marine vehicle projects around the world, we've developed the navigation system for the Hope Turtles from scratch to be fundamentally different from “drone” technology.
turtleos_body_p2: Traditional robotics technology is all about achieving great precision and control— with little thought for the ecosystems, animals, and humans in the environments where they are manufactured, navigated, and discarded. Typically we call such robots "drones" and this is precisely why you won't find that word anywhere else on our site. Its also the reason why we've developed "hope turtles" from the ground up.
turtleos_body_p3: Turtles are gentle and communal. A bunch of turtles is called a "bale"-- and when they work together its never to "swarm" or to attack, its for realizing a collective good. While turtles are famous for being slow-- they are also well known for being methodical and steady-- and coming out winners in the long run! Often bales of adult turtles will arrive en masse to lay eggs on a beach, or babies will simultaneous set out for their first swim. By all working together turtles overwhelm predators by their collective action-- and everyone benefits!
turtleos_body_p4: To emulate this way of being, we've developed turtleOS from the ground up.
turtleos_body_p5: TurtleOS is the brains embedded in every hope turtle's microcontroller. It provides the navigation and mesh communication protocol for turtles to make their way to their destination.
turtleos_body_p6: The code is open source on our github repository. Coded in MicroPython, we explored a whole range of microprocessors and settled on developing specifically for the Xiao ESP32-S3. However, we build on a hardware abstraction layer — which means you can still operate and develop TurtleOS on a Raspberry Pi or an Arduino. TurtleOS is designed to run on our custom developed turtle shell printed circuit board.
turtleos_body_p7: TurtleOS provides not only the navigation algorithm for the deployment of a turtle in the open sea, but also the means to recover detailed sensory telemetry for testing, improvement, and tracking.
turtleos_body_p8: TurtleOS is designed to enable a non-AI logic that is not dependent on any connectivity to migrate on the open seas towards a target 5 to 10 kilometers in size. Using the simplest sensory setup — a GPS and a gyroscope — the turtle can control its sail servo to self-navigate toward its preset heading.
turtleos_body_p9: Rather than precision, turtleOS is about replicability and enhancing collective arrival probabilities. For this reason, while turtles make terrible "swarms" or "mules", they do make a beautiful blessings when they arrive and are discovered by our fellow humans.
turtleos_circuit_alt: TurtleOS circuit development on the Xiao ESP32-S3

turtleos_circuit_caption: Access our TurtleOS code repository. Download and flash your turtle with the latest navigation system.
turtleos_lead: Not a drone — an open-source navigator built to move like a turtle: gentle, communal, and built to arrive.
turtleos_pcb_alt: The Turtle Shell v2.4 printed circuit board
turtleos_pcb_body: Our Turtle Shell Printed Circuit Board (PCP) is what hosts and holds turtleOS. Designed from the ground up to be easy to assemble, inexpensive to produce and perfectly sized to fit into a 1.5L water bottle, our turtle shell holds our hardware stack of microprocessor, navigation instruments and onboard sensors. Our PCB design repository is licensed under a CERN open hardware license and is hosted on gitub.
eco_banner_lead: The regenerative heart of every Hope Turtle — a wood-slat frame that binds food-filled bottles into a seaworthy shell.
eco_banner_login_hint: Login with a Buwana account to use our Turtle Generator
eco_intro_p0: At the heart of Hope Turtle v1 design is an ecojoiner.
eco_intro_p1: Ecojoiners were developed by the Global Ecobrick Alliance as a means to connect bottles into super-practical cubic matrixes for building modular furniture and structures. Ecojoiners go particularly well with ecobricks — however they can work with any bottle as long as it is nice and full. In this way, bottles and ecojoiners can create cubic chairs, tables, shelves, and all sorts of furniture — and they can also serve as the substructure for earth and ecobrick walls.
eco_intro_p2: Over here at the human2human project, we're putting ecojoiners to use for a whole new purpose: holding a turtle's aid-bottles together! It turns out that PET bottles are also fantastic for containing dry food of all kinds in marine conditions.
eco_intro_p3: Using a single ecojoiner, a Hope Turtle can hold five to six 1.5-litre bottles packed with food. We've tested it — and because bottles seal so well, even in sun and sea, they can preserve their contents for weeks!
eco_intro_p4: Knowing the tides and currents, a simple six-bottle turtle can be deployed to float in to its destination.
eco_intro_p5: Optionally, at the top of the turtle, the sixth bottle can be what we call a control bottle: a cut 1.5L PET bottle that houses our specially designed sail mechanism, microcontroller unit, and power system.
eco_intro_p6: The Global Ecobrick Alliance first tried making ecojoiners out of recycled plastic (failure!), then bamboo (way better!), and finally settled on a design that uses wood slats. Unlike bamboo, wood can be sourced just about anywhere in the world. As long as it's the right size — slats from shipping pallets, plywood, or thin boards — it can be transformed with a band saw into a set of flat slats that assemble into our hexa-cube ecojoiner.
eco_note_body: Did you know you can find 85mm 1.5L bottles just about anywhere in the world? Yep — our team has researched it! The brand may vary, but without fail, 1.5L water bottles tend toward a diameter of 85mm. So far we've been able to find matching bottles in pretty much every country we've needed to. This is important: consequently, we've designed our ecojoiners to be compatible with 1.5L bottles with short bottle necks.

turtles_intro_title: What exactly is a Hope Turtle?
turtles_intro_p1: Hope Turtles are a way for anyone, anywhere, to grab local materials and build a marine vehicle that can self-navigate across water to a designated target zone, delivering food and building materials along the way.
turtles_intro_p2: To keep the raw cost of a turtle as low as possible, we've gone out of our way to use locally available materials, simple assembly, and readily available electronics. We've also made every plan and design that makes up a Hope Turtle open source — and better yet, we host an online turtle generator, where you can automatically generate the build files you need to make your own.
turtles_bottles_p1: Like real-life turtles, Hope Turtles come in all shapes and sizes — because they're built with bottles, and bottles come in all shapes and sizes too. Bottles are everywhere in the world today, and though we take them for granted, they're a minor miracle: lightweight, and remarkably good at carrying things while sealing them airtight. As we strive to get much-needed food and medicine to our fellow humans around the world, bottles are ideal for keeping their contents safe.
turtles_design_p1: The core concept of a floating, navigable hope turtle is simple — while our principles are foundational.
turtles_design_p2: This means, following our Earthen design principles, your imagination is the limit on what an actual turtle can look like!
turtles_design_p3: To get started though, after extensive marine testing, we've landed on our v1 core structural design for the Hope Turtle: wood slats and generic 1.5-litre bottles. This keeps us at our goal of having a 95% organic turtle and it keeps assembly and replicability as straightforward as possible. The v1 design uses plain wood slats that are easy for carpenters or CNC machines to cut. There are no moving parts in the body itself. The resulting apparatus holds five 1.5L bottles of food, aid, or medicine, plus one "control bottle" that contains the entire sail-servo, navigation-control, and power-management apparatus in one place.
turtles_design_p4: But our v1 turtle design does more than just deliver food and medicine.
turtles_design_p5: Inspired by the Global Ecobrick Alliance's work developing "ecojoiners" to facilitate bottle construction, we've taken their concept and implemented it into the heart of our v1 turtle.
turtles_design_p6: Ecojoiners were developed by the Global Ecobrick Alliance as a means of assembling bottles into cubic matrices that can be used to build all sorts of things. Ecojoiners have been used with bottles to build chairs, tables, shelves, and more — and we're also very excited about their use as a lattice for earth building, to reinforce cob and adobe structures.
turtles_components_p1: The Hope Turtle Project is made up of four main components. Each has its own GitHub repository, where we maintain and freely share the source code for the project.
turtles_component_body_p1: This is the geometric design of the turtle's body — the structure that holds the bottles. We've taken our CAD files and distilled them into parametric code, which basically means the entire design of the turtle is like one big equation, where the specifics of any bottle determine the size of its various wood slats. That way, right on this site, you can enter the specifics of your bottle and the system will generate the 3D model, carpentry, CNC, and 3D-print files you need to make your turtle.
turtles_component_shell_p1: What's silicone, green, and solid? A turtle shell... and a printed circuit board! That's what we affectionately call our PCBs — the boards that connect the microcontroller, sensors, and power together to run the turtle. Every component we've used is easy to find, off-the-shelf, and inexpensive: you can source them from online electronics markets in just about any country for under $30, or have the PCB itself printed by any online service for about $5. Soon, you'll even be able to order the PCB directly from us — we're printing them in batches.
turtles_component_os_p1: We've developed, from the ground up, a navigation system to run our turtles: TurtleOS. With a single terminal command, you can install it on any off-the-shelf Xiao ESP32-S3 and be up and running with your turtle in no time. TurtleOS orchestrates the onboard sensors, lets you pick a destination, and sets your turtle swimming. It uses the microcontroller's on-board wifi to connect via API to hopeturtles.org — so with a free account, you can track and monitor your turtle's progress.
turtles_component_site_p1: This site is open source too! We've put the full code stack up on GitHub for collaborative development. Our site — gratefully hosted by DewaWeb in Indonesia — is what you're using right now. With a free Buwana account, you can sign up and log in to manage your turtles, and connect bottles, missions, boats, and more. This is also where our turtle generator lives, connecting directly to the Turtle Body's programmatic geometry so you can generate your own turtle based on your local bottles and wood.
gen_page_title: Generate Your Turtle Components — Hope Turtle Structure
gen_hero_blurb: Our hope turtles are made out of various components that are specific to the PET bottles that you choose for your project. Our Turtle Generator system lets you choose a turtle design (we only have the v1 at the moment!) then input your bottle's dimensions and generate the custom design files you will need to build it. Choose from 2D carpentry specs, 3D SCAD renders, CNC cutting files, to SVG 1:1 outlines. This is a non-AI, 100% algorithmic generation of the turtle component geometry. The generated files serve as a starting point for customizing your turtle's design to the quirks of your local bottle.

gen_login_required_body: Generating and saving turtle component files requires a free Ecobricks/Buwana account, since your bottle profiles and designs are saved to your dashboard. Log in or sign up to get started.
contribute_banner_lead: Every contribution helps launch and maintain a fleet of Hope Turtles.
contribute_body_p1: Hope Turtles are a non-capital technology. This means they are designed from the ground up not to rely on capital-intensive platforms, technologies or components. Yes, money is still important, but it is not central. In fact, the biggest contribution you can make is not to send us money, but to use it to build your own turtle using the plans and code which we make available here — along with local wood, bottles, food-stuffs and readily available basic electronics.
contribute_body_p2: Of course, developing and maintaining the technological and conceptual infrastructure of the project has its costs — and we welcome you commissioning us to manifest a turtle for you, or to order some of the components we've developed, to put to use in your own locale.
contribute_body_p3: In this way, Hope Turtles can unfold without the impediments of financial barriers, as a fully collaborative project powered by many small contributions rather than a few big ones. That said, it's worth pointing out that we are not sponsored by any governments or institutions. When it comes to capital, we believe in full transparency, and we publish all our accounting in our OpenBooks accounting system.
gen_p1_desc: Choose the perfect local bottle for your turtle component
gen_p1_body: Choosing the correct bottle type for your turtle (and future constructions with turtles and bottles!) is key. Not all bottles are ideal. The best tend to be tall and thin, rather than short and stubby. Crucial is that the bottles have short top and bottom tappers and have bodies with flat, upright sides. You can use any bottle size, but for the moment we are recommending 1.5L bottles that are between 83mm and 87mm in diameter. Our research shows that type of generic water bottle size is pretty consistent around the world.
gen_p1_alt: Choosing the right bottle for a turtle component
gen_p2_desc: Specify the key dimensions of your bottle
gen_p2_body: Bottles come in all shapes and sizes. Turtle components must adapt! Please measure carefully the key dimensions of your bottle and set them here. All dimensions are in millimetres (mm).
gen_p3_desc: Turtle components can be built from just about anything flat
gen_p3_body: Turtle components are best built with organic material that is between 8mm and 25mm thick. The best for ocean durability is solid wood boards. Do not use plastic as it will degrade into polluting the ocean and shore. Avoid metal as it will decrease buoyancy.

build_page_title: Build Your Own Hope Turtle — Hope Turtle Tutorial
build_notice_body: Some steps are still being built out — we'll mark them as they come online. 🐢
build_hero_p1: The Hope Turtle is designed from the ground up to be built by anyone, anywhere, for under €100. Its body is wood, bottles and food; its brain is an off-the-shelf microcontroller; and everything about it — the 3D models, the carpentry generator, the circuit board, the navigation software and this very website — is open source.
build_hero_p2: Our work is meant to be the foundation, not the final word. Take it, build it, and then make it better: adapt the design to the bottles you can find, the wood you can source and the winds and waters of your region — and share what you learn so the next turtle swims further.
build_s1_desc: Choose your bottle, then let the generator draw your turtle's wooden parts.
build_s1_p1: Every Hope Turtle starts with a bottle. The wooden frame — the 6FC Ecojoiner core, the rear fin, the ballast fin and the sails — is sized around the exact bottle you'll be using, so pick one you can find plenty of locally: a sturdy, straight-sided PET bottle (1.5 L is our reference) whose cap and collar are consistent from bottle to bottle. You'll need one for the control bottle and several more for food.
build_s1_p2: Measure it carefully with calipers — diameter, height, cap, collar and the tapers at the top and bottom — then enter those numbers into our Turtle Generator, along with the thickness of the boards you'll use. The generator is 100% algorithmic: it applies the turtle_body design rules to your measurements and hands back a set of files for each component.
build_s1_table_caption: What the generator gives you, and what to do with it
build_s1_row_carpentry_use: Print the carpenter sheets: every part dimensioned, with hole positions and quantities. Mark them out on your boards and cut with hand or power tools.
build_s1_row_cnc_use: 1:1 vector outlines with holes. Import into your CAM software, set your toolpaths and route the parts from sheet stock.
build_s1_row_laser_use: 1:1 outlines for a laser cutter (or printed as full-size paper templates). Needs a powerful laser for 12 mm boards.
build_s1_row_3d_use: The parametric OpenSCAD model. Open in OpenSCAD to preview the parts in 3D, tweak them, or export STL for printing.
build_s2_desc: Turn your blueprints into real wooden parts.
build_s2_carpentry_body: Our recommended path, and the one the whole design is built around. All you need is a saw, a drill, a ruler, a square and some clamps — tools found in almost every village and town on earth. Print the PDF carpenter sheets, mark each part onto your boards (pallet wood and offcuts work well), cut, then drill the holes. It's slower than a machine and asks for care with your measurements, but it costs next to nothing, needs no electricity beyond a drill, and anyone can learn it. Cut one test joint first to check the fit with your bottle before cutting the full set.
build_s2_cnc_body: If you have access to a CNC router — at a makerspace, a sign shop or a furniture workshop — the DXF files will give you fast, perfectly repeatable parts, which is ideal if you're building several turtles. Import the DXF into your CAM software, set tabs so parts don't fly loose, and compensate for your bit diameter on the inside slots. The downsides: the machines are expensive, need some CAM know-how, and want flat, consistent sheet material like plywood rather than reclaimed boards.
build_s2_laser_body: A laser cutter gives crisp, precise edges straight from the SVG files and is great for prototyping at small scale — try cutting the parts from cardboard or thin ply to check your fit. But the turtle's structure is designed around 12 mm boards, which most hobby lasers can't cut through cleanly; you'll need a high-power CO₂ machine, and you'll get charred edges that should be sanded. Laser-printed paper templates are a good hybrid: cut them out and trace them onto wood for carpentry.
build_s2_3d_body: Technically possible — you can export STLs from the SCAD files — but we don't recommend 3D printing the wooden frame. The parts are large, slow and costly to print, and a plastic structure goes against the turtle's regenerative, mostly-organic design. Use the SCAD model instead to preview and customise your design in OpenSCAD. Save your printer for the small, precise parts of Step 3, where it truly shines.
build_s3_desc: 3D-print the turtle_body v1 parts that turn a bottle into the turtle's steering heart.
build_s3_p1: The control bottle is the one bottle in your turtle that holds no food: it holds the electronics and drives the sail. Its parts need precision and waterproofing that wood can't give, so they're 3D-printed from the open-source turtle_body v1 STL files. Here's what you'll print:
build_s3_cage_body: The rotating cage that sits on top of the control cap and rides on eight bearing bumps. The sail battens bolt into its grooves, so when the cage turns, the sail turns.
build_s3_cap_body: The large stationary disk that seals into the cut-open control bottle. Its central bore carries the sail shaft through an O-ring gland, keeping the electronics inside dry.
build_s3_mold_body: A two-part press mould for casting your own silicone seals: the flat rings that seal the cap insert to the bottle, and the small O-rings that seal the spinning shaft.
build_s3_shaft_body: The round axle that connects the sail cage to the inside of the bottle. A magnet in its lower end lets the turtle's angle sensor read exactly where the sail is pointing.
build_s3_gear_body: The internal frame that will hold the motor and gearing that turn the shaft and steer the sail.
build_s3_p2: These files are currently sized for our reference bottle. We're building a tool that will generate them for your bottle.
build_s4_desc: Pull together the turtle's hardware stack on its Turtle Shell.
build_s4_p1: Now for the turtle's brain and nervous system. The hardware stack is built around a Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 microcontroller, joined by a GPS module, a real-time clock, a battery and power monitor, the magnetic angle sensor that reads the sail shaft, the motor driver that turns it, and a small solar panel to keep everything charged. All of it plugs into the Turtle Shell — our open-source printed circuit board that connects, powers and protects the electronics so they can be tucked neatly inside the control bottle.
build_s4_p2: There are two ways to get your Turtle Shell:
build_s4_opt1_body: A ready-made Turtle Shell, shipped to you from the Hope Turtle Project.
build_s4_opt2_body: The Turtle Shell's plans are fully open source. Send the Gerber and pick-and-place files to a PCB manufacturer such as JLCPCB or PCBWay in China and have a batch printed and assembled to order.
build_s4_p3: With your shell in hand, solder on the headers, seat the XIAO and modules, connect the battery, solar panel and motor leads, and test that everything powers up before it goes into the bottle.
build_s5_desc: Wood, bottles, printed parts and circuits become one turtle.
build_s5_p1: This is the moment it all becomes a turtle. Start with the 6FC Ecojoiner from Step 1: the Long Johns, Little Johns and Final Keys lock together around your bottles, with the deeper-slotted Master John sprung in last to close the frame. The bottles slot into its ports and are held fast by the pressers.
build_s5_p2: Fit the control bottle from Step 3 in the central position, with your Turtle Shell from Step 4 sealed inside and the shaft rising through the control cap. Seat the cage on top, then bolt the sail frame — top bar, battens and bottom bars — to the cage so the sail swings as the shaft turns.
build_s5_p3: Finally, attach the rear fin with its solar-panel holder at the back, and the ballast fin underneath to keep your turtle upright and tracking straight. Check every bolt, spin the sail by hand to make sure it moves freely, and float-test your turtle in a bucket, pool or calm water before it goes anywhere near the sea.
build_s6_desc: Give your turtle its brain — and connect it to your hopeturtles.org account.
build_s6_p1: TurtleOS is the open-source navigation software that runs your turtle. To install it, you'll need a free Buwana account on hopeturtles.org. Log in, register your turtle from your dashboard, and you'll be given its device ID and device key — the credentials your turtle uses to report its position back to this site.
build_s6_p2: Then plug your XIAO ESP32-S3 into your computer by USB and run the TurtleOS install script in a terminal. It will walk you through flashing MicroPython, then ask for your wifi details and your device keys, write them into your turtle's configuration and install the latest TurtleOS. Keep your device key private — it's what proves to hopeturtles.org that your turtle is really yours.
build_s6_cta_login: Log in to get your device keys
build_s7_desc: Fill the rest of the turtle with something worth delivering.
build_s7_p1: The rest of the turtle's bottles are its cargo — and its buoyancy. Wash and fully dry each bottle (any moisture left inside will spoil the food), fill it with a dry good, and seal the cap tightly. A strip of tape or a dab of wax over the cap adds an extra seal against the sea.
build_s7_p3: The key is to pack every bottle tight. Fill a little, then tap and shake the bottle to settle the contents, and repeat until it's packed right to the top with no air gap. A tightly packed bottle is rigid and strong, keeps its shape against the waves, can't slosh or shift the turtle's balance, and leaves no room for air and moisture to spoil the food. A loosely packed bottle dents, rattles and rots.
build_s8_desc: Your turtle's remote control, in your pocket.
build_s8_p1: The Turtle Wrangler is our Android app for working with your turtle in the field. It will be available on the Google Play Store soon.
build_s8_p2: Standing next to your turtle, open the Wrangler, connect to it, and set its two most important coordinates: its Departure — the point it's setting out from — and its Destination, the shore you want it to reach. Pick each one on the map or drop a pin at your current location. The Wrangler sends them to TurtleOS, which uses them to steer the sail toward the destination for the rest of the journey. Then check your turtle's battery, GPS fix and sail sensor before you say goodbye.
build_s8_coming_soon: Coming soon to the Play Store
build_s9_desc: Set your turtle free yourself, or send it to join a flotilla.
build_s9_deploy_body: Wait for a windy day when the wind is blowing steadily from your departure point toward your destination — check a local wind forecast, and never launch into an onshore wind that will push your turtle straight back to the beach. Make sure your turtle is powered on and has a GPS fix, carry it out past the breaking waves (by kayak or boat if you can), point it downwind and let it go. Stay a few minutes to watch it find its course.
build_s9_deliver_body: Not near the right coast, or want your turtle to travel with others? Pack it up — remove the sail and fins, wrap the control bottle to protect the electronics, and box the parts securely — then deliver or ship it to a flotilla reception point. There it will be checked, reassembled and launched alongside other turtles on a community arribada mission, all setting out together toward the same destination.
build_s10_desc: Follow your turtle across the water.
build_s10_p1: Once your turtle is swimming, it will report its position, battery and sensor readings whenever it can connect. Follow its journey live on hopeturtles.org — from your dashboard or on the mission map — or in the Turtle Wrangler app. And when your turtle reaches shore, whoever finds it can report the arrival here, closing the loop on its journey.
build_footer_body: Found a better joint, a better seal or a better bottle? Every part of the Hope Turtle is open source — share your improvements on GitHub and help the next builder.
cbgen_page_title: Generate Your Control Bottle — Hope Turtle
cbgen_notice_body: We're laying out the control bottle generator now — file generation will be switched on in the next update. 🙏
cbgen_hero_blurb: The control bottle is the steering heart of your turtle: the one bottle that holds the electronics and turns the sail. Its parts are 3D-printed from the open-source turtle_body v1 models, and each one is sized to the bottle it fits. Choose one of your saved bottle profiles or enter the specs of a new bottle, pick the components you want, and we'll generate the SCAD and STL files ready for your printer.
cbgen_p1_desc: Use a saved bottle profile, or start a new one.
cbgen_p1_body: Your control bottle should be the same type of bottle as the rest of your turtle, so the control cap seats properly in the 6FC Ecojoiner. If you've already made blueprints with the Turtle Generator, choose that bottle profile and its measurements will be filled in for you.
cbgen_no_profiles: You don't have any saved bottle profiles yet. Enter your bottle below — or save one from the Turtle Generator.
cbgen_p2_desc: Measure your bottle to the nearest tenth of a millimetre.
cbgen_p2_body: Measure with calipers, in millimetres. The control cap's insert is cut to fit the inside of your bottle, so the diameter and wall thickness matter most — a 0.5 mm error is the difference between a watertight seal and a leak.
cbgen_field_cut_height_hint: Where you'll cut the bottle open, measured from the base.
cbgen_p3_desc: Pick which control bottle parts to generate.
cbgen_p3_body: You'll need all of these for your first control bottle. If you're re-printing a part that broke or wore out, just pick that one.
cbgen_part_cage_desc: The rotating cage that sits on the control cap and carries the sail battens.
cbgen_part_cap_desc: The stationary disk that seals into the cut bottle and holds the shaft's O-ring gland.
cbgen_part_mold_desc: A two-part press mould for casting the cap's flat seals and the shaft's O-rings.
cbgen_part_shaft_desc: The axle that links the cage to the inside of the bottle, with a recess for the angle-sensing magnet.
cbgen_part_servo_desc: The internal frame that holds the servo that turns the shaft and steers the sail.
cbgen_p4_desc: Tune the fit to your printer and choose your files.
cbgen_p4_body: Every printer prints a little differently. If your parts usually come out snug, add some clearance; if they come out loose, reduce it. Standard suits most well-calibrated FDM printers.
cbgen_fmt_stl_desc: Slice and print straight away. One file per component.
cbgen_fmt_scad_desc: The parametric OpenSCAD model, for tweaking the design yourself.
cbgen_submit_pending: Thanks for testing! File generation isn't switched on yet — it's coming in the next update.
cbgen_login_title: Log in to generate your control bottle
cbgen_login_body: Your control bottle is sized to your bottle, so this generator works from the bottle profiles saved to your hopeturtles.org account — the same ones you use in the Turtle Generator. Log in or sign up for a free Buwana account to get started.
cbgen_login_point2: Generate the cage, cap, O-ring mould and shaft
cbgen_login_point3: Download print-ready STL and editable SCAD files
